lessons.title: Short tracks
lessons.objective: Describe what makes short tracks different.

payload.prompt: What is the defining characteristic of a short track in NASCAR?

options.text: Under a mile around.
No banking at all.
Only two turns instead of four.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Short tracks are under a mile around, like Martinsville and Bristol. One-mile ovals such as Phoenix sit on the border and race like big short tracks.
explanation.incorrect: Short tracks are the small ovals, under a mile around. Banking varies from low at Martinsville to steep at Bristol, but every oval has four turns.

payload.prompt: Which one is a short-track oval?

image.alt: Three track shapes: left is a tiny oval with sharp turns; middle is a large oval; right is a road course with multiple turns and straights.

options.text: The compact oval on the left
The larger oval in the middle
The road course on the right

cues: Short tracks are tight and compact, with sharp turns and short straightaways.

explanation.correct: Right. Right. That tight, compact oval is the short-track shape: bumper-to-bumper racing.
explanation.incorrect: Short tracks are compact ovals under a mile, like Bristol (0.533 miles) and Martinsville (0.526 miles). The shape is tight, not a sprawling giant oval.

payload.prompt: Match the track to what it is known for.

pairs.definition: A 0.533-mile concrete oval with steep banking, known for loud, bumper-to-bumper racing.
A 0.526-mile paperclip with little banking, where contact is expected.
A one-mile, low-banked oval that races like a big short track.

distractorDefinitions: A long intermediate over two miles known for speed.
A superspeedway over 2.5 miles with drafting.

explanation.summary: Short tracks reward contact skills, patience and tire management. They are where payback happens.

payload.prompt: Complete the short-track description.
payload.template: Short tracks are known for {{style}} racing because cars run {{proximity}}.

explanation.correct: Right. There is no room to run alone at Bristol or Martinsville.
explanation.incorrect: Short-track racing is defined by tight proximity: cars run bumper-to-bumper, and contact is part of the game. Passing requires aggressive moves.

payload.prompt: At a short track, does the fastest car always win?

scene.alt: Aerial view of Bristol Motor Speedway showing its compact oval shape with two tight turns.

choices.label: No, racecraft and tires matter too
Yes, speed is the only thing

explanation.correct: Right. Short tracks reward racecraft, patience and tire management as well as raw speed.
explanation.incorrect: Short tracks are racecraft tracks. Speed matters, but so do tire management, handling traffic and contact. A smart driver often beats a faster car.

lessons.title: Intermediates
lessons.objective: Explain why intermediates are about aero and handling.

payload.prompt: How long is a typical intermediate track?

options.text: Between 1 and 2 miles.
Exactly 1.5 miles, all of them.
Over 2.5 miles, always.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Intermediates range from about 1.0 to 2.0 miles: Charlotte, Las Vegas, Kansas, Michigan.
explanation.incorrect: Intermediate tracks are 1-2 miles. Not all are the same length, but they share the characteristic of being the 'middle rung' between short and superspeedway.

payload.prompt: Match the intermediate concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: How much a car's speed depends on airflow: higher at intermediate and superspeedway tracks, lower at short tracks.
Aerodynamic pressure that pushes the car to the track, improving grip in the corners.
Air resistance that slows the car; a tradeoff when adding downforce for better turning.
How the car responds to the driver's inputs; aero-sensitive tracks demand precise setup.

distractorDefinitions: The fuel consumption at a given speed.
The tire compound used only at intermediates.

explanation.summary: Intermediates demand that teams get aero and setup exactly right because speed is so sensitive to both.

payload.prompt: How long is Charlotte Motor Speedway?

explanation.correct: Close. Charlotte is 1.5 miles, a classic intermediate.
explanation.incorrect: Charlotte Motor Speedway is 1.5 miles: right in the intermediate range. Intermediates run from about 1 mile to 2 (Michigan), and 1.5 miles is the most common length.

payload.prompt: What matters more at intermediates than at short tracks?
payload.template: At intermediates, {{factor}} matters more than at short tracks.

explanation.correct: Right. Aero is king at intermediates.
explanation.incorrect: Intermediate tracks are aerodynamic-sensitive: clean air, dirty air, spoiler height, splitter angle. Small changes in aero setup ripple through the entire race.

payload.prompt: Is being in clean air more important at intermediates than at short tracks?

scene.alt: Aerial view of a 1.5-mile oval showing two cars: one in front with clear air, one directly behind in the leader's draft wake.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Aero-sensitive intermediates reward clean air heavily because the car behind loses lots of grip.
explanation.incorrect: Intermediates are all about aerodynamics. Being in clean air at an intermediate is a massive advantage; dirty air ruins your pace.

payload.prompt: What sets a superspeedway race apart?

options.text: Cars run flat out in big packs and the draft decides passing.
Cars run single file because passing is banned.
Cars brake hard into tight hairpins.

explanation.correct: Right. Daytona (2.5 miles), Talladega (2.66 miles) and Atlanta (1.54 miles, but raced the same way) are where pack racing rules.
explanation.incorrect: Superspeedways are the big, high-banked ovals where cars run wide open in packs and the draft dominates. Passing is allowed, so there is no single-file rule, and there are no hairpins.

payload.prompt: How long is Daytona International Speedway?

explanation.correct: Exactly. Daytona is 2.5 miles, the most famous superspeedway.
explanation.incorrect: Daytona International Speedway is 2.5 miles with steeply banked oval turns and a tri-oval front stretch.

payload.prompt: How much power at superspeedways in 2026?
payload.template: In 2026, Cup cars make about {{horsepower}} at superspeedways.

explanation.correct: Right. The smaller tapered spacer at Daytona and Talladega limits power for safety.
explanation.incorrect: Superspeedways use about 510 horsepower, through a smaller tapered spacer, to keep pack speeds in check. It is the lowest power level of the season.

payload.prompt: Match the superspeedway concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A front stretch with a gentle bend that gives the track a three-cornered shape, as at Daytona and Talladega.
The tilt of the racing surface; high banking at Daytona and Talladega lets cars run faster.
Many cars running nose-to-tail because the draft equalizes speed.
How much faster one car is than another; small at superspeedways because the draft evens speeds out.

distractorDefinitions: A low-banking flat surface for mechanical grip.
A road course with left and right turns.

explanation.summary: Superspeedways are the domain of pack racing, where strategy and luck matter as much as speed.

payload.prompt: Can the draft help a trailing car catch the leader?

scene.alt: Side-by-side view of a superspeedway finish with multiple cars running nose-to-tail at the line.

choices.label: Yes, it gives the trailer a run
No, it holds the trailer back

explanation.correct: Correct. The trailing car gets a run from the tow and can pull alongside. The leader can block, so it becomes a game of timing.
explanation.incorrect: The draft bunches cars and gives the trailer extra speed, so it can close on the leader. It does not hold the trailer back.

lessons.title: Road courses and the Roval
lessons.objective: Explain what makes road courses different.

payload.prompt: Which track layout is a road course?

image.alt: Three track layouts: left is a simple oval; middle is a complex course with multiple left and right turns, straights and chicanes; right is another oval with one banked turn.

options.text: The simple oval on the left
The complex circuit in the middle
The banked turn on the right

cues: Road courses have left and right turns, multiple chicanes and varying elevation.

explanation.correct: Right. Sonoma and Watkins Glen are road courses: precise braking and hitting the apex matter.
explanation.incorrect: Road courses are left-and-right circuits with braking zones and elevation changes. NASCAR runs several road courses, such as Sonoma and Watkins Glen, plus the Charlotte Roval.

payload.prompt: Why can road-course specialists sometimes beat faster Cup cars?

options.text: Road courses reward braking and apex precision more than top speed.
Road cars and race cars are the same thing.
Cup cars are not allowed to use the full engine power.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A road-course ringer can out-brake and out-apex drivers with raw speed but less technical skill.
explanation.incorrect: Road courses are about braking, apexes and patience, not just engine power. A driver skilled in threshold braking and line precision can beat a faster car with cruder skills.

payload.prompt: Match the road-course term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Where drivers slow for a corner; braking later is how most road-course passes are made.
The tightest point of a turn; hitting it perfectly means the most speed on exit.
How fast a driver leaves a corner onto the next straight; small differences compound into gaps.
Charlotte's hybrid track: a road course laid over the oval's infield plus one banked turn.

distractorDefinitions: The starting position in a road-course race.
The fuel used only at road courses.

explanation.summary: Road courses punish mistakes harshly: a tenth lost on exit carries through the whole lap.

payload.prompt: You are behind a slower car into a road-course braking zone. Dive?

facts.label: Your car
facts.value: Quicker on the brakes and through the corner

facts.label: Race position
facts.value: Late in the race, points matter

options.label: Dive for the inside from way back
options.consequence: You are too far back to get alongside, so you lock the brakes, run wide or take the other car out.
considerations: Three car lengths is too far back for a move to stick.
A failed dive usually costs you and the car ahead.

options.label: Close up, then pass at the next braking zone
options.consequence: You stay close on the exit, get a run and brake later at the next corner, making a clean pass.
considerations: A good exit sets up the next braking zone.
A clean pass beats a risky dive.

options.label: Stay back and hope for a mistake
options.consequence: You keep the car clean, but you are not working to get by and may run out of laps.
considerations: Waiting only works if the other driver errs.
Sometimes track position is worth holding.

payload.expertNote: Road-course passing is about a good exit and a late brake, not a lunge from far back.

payload.prompt: Is the Charlotte Roval a road course or an oval?

scene.alt: Aerial view of the Charlotte Roval showing the road course infield layout plus one banked oval turn.

explanation.correct: Right. The Roval is unique: road-course precision plus one high-speed banked oval turn.
explanation.incorrect: The Charlotte Roval is a hybrid: a road course carved into the oval's infield, plus one banked turn on the oval portion. It requires both skill sets.

lessons.title: Banking, grooves and rubber
lessons.objective: Choose the groove for the situation.

payload.prompt: Tap the high-banking turn.

diagram.alt: Side-by-side cross-sections of two turns: left shows a sharp tilt (high banking); right shows an almost flat surface (low banking).

explanation.correct: Exactly. Steep banking, like Bristol's, tilts the turn so cars can carry much more speed through it.
explanation.incorrect: Steep banking tilts the turn toward the infield so the track helps hold the car in, which lets it go faster. Low banking is nearly flat, like Martinsville or Phoenix.

payload.prompt: What is rubbering in?

options.text: Rubber from tire friction building up in the fast groove, making it grippier.
Adding extra rubber to the tires before the race.
A penalty for excessive brake dust.

explanation.correct: Right. As the race goes on, tires rubber in the fast line, and sometimes a higher or lower groove opens up.
explanation.incorrect: Rubbering in is the process of tire rubber accumulating on the track in the fastest groove, making it even grippier. Late in a race, a new groove might become competitive as rubber spreads.

payload.prompt: What do low-banked tracks demand?
payload.template: Low-banked tracks like Martinsville and Phoenix demand {{skill}} because there is little {{resource}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Low-banked tracks cannot be muscled with speed; setup and driver skill do the work.
explanation.incorrect: Low-banked tracks like Martinsville and Phoenix give the turn little help, so drivers rely on tire grip and setup. Speed through a flat turn takes precision, not just horsepower.

payload.prompt: Does the fastest groove always stay the same throughout a race?

scene.alt: Top-down view of a turn showing rubber buildup in the low line early race, and in the high line by mid-race.

choices.label: No, rubber migration opens new lines.

explanation.correct: Right. As rubber lays down, grooves can shift from low to high, or new lines open up.
explanation.incorrect: The fast groove moves as the race evolves. Early on the bottom might be best; later the top can become faster as rubber builds up. Drivers who adapt have an edge.

payload.prompt: Why does drafting work in stock car racing?

options.text: The car behind runs lower air pressure in its tires.
The lead car cuts through the air, and the trailer meets less resistance.
Drafting is a rule that lets the second-place car borrow power.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The lead car pushes aside the air; the trailer slips through the reduced-resistance zone behind.
explanation.incorrect: Drafting is pure physics: the lead car's slipstream reduces aerodynamic drag for the car behind, letting it go faster without more throttle. Both cars go faster when in a draft pair or line.

payload.prompt: How close must you run to get the tow?
payload.template: A drafting car must run {{proximity}} the leader to gain the tow.

explanation.correct: Right. The draft works when you are very close; distance kills the effect.
explanation.incorrect: Drafting is a close-range effect. You need to be right behind the lead car, within a car length or two, to feel the drag reduction. Farther back the air has closed up again.

payload.prompt: Match the drafting term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Running nose-to-tail behind another car to reduce your own aerodynamic drag.
The turbulent air and reduced-pressure zone directly behind a car.
The speed bonus you gain from drafting a car.
The air resistance that slows a car; the lead car fights this; the trailer is shielded.

distractorDefinitions: A fuel-saving technique at short tracks.

explanation.summary: Drafting is nearly free speed. The catch is that you are running close behind another car, so its moves quickly become yours.

payload.prompt: Does the lead car also benefit from a draft line?

scene.alt: Side view of two cars in close proximity; the lead car is shown facing air turbulence; the trailing car is shielded.

choices.label: Yes, both cars go faster in a line.

explanation.correct: Right. A car tucked right behind fills in the low-pressure wake, so the leader loses some drag too, and a line of cars outruns a lone car.
explanation.incorrect: In a draft line, every car gains some speed. The lead car still punches the most air, but a line runs faster than cars spread out alone. That is why packs form at superspeedways.

lessons.title: Clean air and dirty air
lessons.objective: Explain why the leader has clean air and the follower loses grip.

payload.prompt: At an intermediate, is it easy to pass a leader while stuck in dirty air?

scene.alt: Overhead view of two cars on an intermediate oval: the lead car has undisturbed air in front; the trailer is engulfed in the lead car's disturbed wake.

choices.label: No, dirty air costs front grip
Yes, a faster car just drives by

explanation.correct: Exactly. Dirty air can be so costly that a faster car cannot get by.
explanation.incorrect: At aero-sensitive tracks, dirty air is poison. The turbulent wake behind the lead car takes downforce off the trailer's nose, so the trailer cannot turn well enough to make a pass.

payload.prompt: What is dirty air?

options.text: Exhaust fumes from the car ahead.
Turbulent air behind another car that reduces front grip.
A malfunction in the radiator cooling system.

explanation.correct: Right. Dirty air is the disturbed, turbulent wake; it kills downforce.
explanation.incorrect: Dirty air is the turbulent airflow directly behind a car. It takes downforce off the nose of the car following, which usually makes it tight, as if it will not turn.

payload.prompt: Why can a leader hold off a faster car?
payload.template: A leader in clean air can hold off a faster car because the car behind is stuck {{where}} and loses {{what}}.

explanation.correct: Right. In dirty air the follower loses front grip, so track position and clean air can beat a faster car.
explanation.incorrect: At aero-sensitive tracks, the car in front has clean air and the car behind loses front grip in its wake. That is why being in front can be worth more than a little extra speed.

payload.prompt: Match the air concept to what it means.

pairs.definition: Smooth, undisturbed airflow on the nose and splitter; the lead car has it.
Turbulent wake behind another car that reduces grip and speed.
The disturbed air pattern left behind a car at speed.
Where you run in the field, which decides who gets the clean air.

distractorDefinitions: The penalty for exceeding pit road speed.

explanation.summary: Clean air can be worth more than raw speed. Fans say track position is king because of clean and dirty air.

lessons.title: Bump drafts and side drafts
lessons.objective: Distinguish bump draft from side draft.

payload.prompt: Match the draft technique to its execution.

pairs.definition: A trailing car touches the lead car's bumper, which can speed both for a moment; risky at speed.
Running alongside another car to disturb the air on its side, slowing it or making it unstable.
Extra speed from the draft that lets a trailing car pull alongside the one ahead.
Follow closely behind another car to use its draft.

distractorDefinitions: A penalty flag thrown at the start.
The fuel mixture used in cold weather.

explanation.summary: Drafting moves range from tucking in behind a car to bumping or side drafting it. Each has a reward and a risk.

payload.prompt: Why is a bump draft risky?

options.text: The lead car might lose control and wreck both cars.
It is always illegal and brings an automatic penalty.
Bump drafts only work in the rain.

explanation.correct: Right. Touching at speed can destabilize either car.
explanation.incorrect: A bump draft at 180+ mph is contact at high speed. If the lead car gets loose or turns wrong, both cars can wreck. That is why drivers save it for moments that matter, such as the final lap.

payload.prompt: What does a side draft do to the other car?
payload.template: In a side draft, a car running {{where}} another disturbs its air and can {{effect}}.

options: slow it or make it unstable
gaps.correct: slow it or make it unstable

explanation.correct: Right. Air is pushed and disturbed between two cars running side by side, which can take grip and speed from the other car.
explanation.incorrect: A side draft works through the air between cars running side by side. The disturbed air can slow the other car or unsettle it, with no bumper contact needed.

payload.prompt: Does a side draft need bumper contact?

scene.alt: Two-car view: left shows a bump draft (car nudging the bumper); right shows a side draft (cars running side-by-side with airflow interaction).

choices.label: Yes, the cars must touch bumpers
No, it works through the air

explanation.correct: Right. A side draft works through air between cars running side by side. Only the bump draft starts with a tap, though both carry risk at 180 mph.
explanation.incorrect: A side draft is about airflow, not contact. Cars run alongside and the disturbed air does the work, while a bump draft is an actual tap on the bumper.

lessons.title: Packs and the Big One
lessons.objective: Pick lanes in a pack and see how the Big One starts.

payload.prompt: What typically starts the Big One?

options.text: A single mistake in a tight pack that spreads instantly.
An intentional crash by a frustrated driver.
A rule violation that triggers a caution flag.

explanation.correct: Exactly. One car gets loose or taps another; the pack is so tight that everyone crashes trying to avoid it.
explanation.incorrect: The Big One is a chain-reaction wreck in a superspeedway pack. One small mistake—a tap, a lift—causes the car behind to swerve; that hits the car behind that, and suddenly a dozen cars are crashing.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Talladega, so bring the Big One.

options.text: A multi-car wreck is a real possibility today.
One car will win by a big margin.
Bring a bigger engine than usual.

payload.translation: Superspeedway pack racing is risky; expect a big crash.

followUps.line: Is the Big One just bad luck?
followUps.why: Not really. Packs form naturally from the draft, so one mistake can ripple through dozens of cars. Asking shows you get the structure.

followUps.line: Do some drivers just ride at the back to stay out of it?
followUps.why: Some do, and fans understand it. Staying clear of a wreck can be a real strategy, even if it costs track position.

payload.prompt: Match the superspeedway term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Many cars running nose-to-tail and side-by-side because drafting speeds are equal.
Picking high or low based on which line has momentum at the moment.
Momentum built by a line of cars; a run swings from one lane to the other.
A multi-car superspeedway crash caused by one small mistake in a tight pack.

distractorDefinitions: A solo victory by the fastest car.
A penalty for blocking too aggressively.

explanation.summary: Superspeedway racing is about lanes, momentum and reading the moment. Luck and survival matter as much as speed.

payload.prompt: Tenth at Talladega, three to go. The high lane has a run. Go?

facts.label: High lane momentum
facts.value: A fast line of 4 cars is pushing up track

facts.label: Low lane status
facts.value: Stalled; cars there are losing ground

options.label: Go with the run on the high lane
options.consequence: You ride the momentum and can gain several spots before the flag, though a pack this tight can also wreck.
considerations: A run is momentum you can use right now.
With three laps left there is little time to wait.
Risk is higher, but so is the reward.

options.label: Stay low and protect tenth
options.consequence: You likely finish around tenth, avoiding the worst of the risk but giving up the chance to gain spots.
considerations: A safe top-ten finish still earns good points.
A stalled lane loses spots as others pass.
Top five needs a bolder move.

options.label: Sit in the middle between lanes
options.consequence: You lose the push from both lanes and can get squeezed or shuffled backward.
considerations: A pack has no free middle lane.
Commit to one line so the cars around you know where you are.

payload.expertNote: Superspeedway racing rewards reading the moment and committing. A run may only last a lap or two.

lessons.title: Name that track
lessons.objective: Identify a track by its shape.

payload.prompt: Which track is this?

image.alt: Overhead outline of a very large tri-oval: a long, gently bent front stretch, wide sweeping turns and a long backstretch.

options.text: Daytona International Speedway
Bristol Motor Speedway
Martinsville Speedway

cues: Look for the bent tri-oval front stretch and the big, wide turns.

explanation.correct: Right. Daytona is the big tri-oval home of the Daytona 500.
explanation.incorrect: Daytona International Speedway is 2.5 miles with a tri-oval front stretch and high banking. Bristol is a small bowl and Martinsville a tiny paperclip, so neither looks like this.

payload.prompt: If a driver is great at Martinsville but terrible at Daytona, what does that suggest?

options.text: Short-track skills do not translate to superspeedway pack racing.
That driver has a mechanical problem at Daytona.
All drivers should be equally good at every track.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Different track types reward different skills, and short-track racecraft is not the same as pack racing.
explanation.incorrect: Different track types reward different skills. A short-track ace excels at contact and tires, while superspeedway pack racing is about drafting, lanes and patience.

payload.prompt: Match the crown jewel to its significance.

pairs.definition: The most prestigious race, run in February at Daytona; a win launches a career.
A 600-mile race at Charlotte Motor Speedway; one of the longest and most grueling.
Darlington's historic race, known for its egg-shaped, tricky track.
The Cup race at Indianapolis, the speedway that also hosts the Indy 500.

distractorDefinitions: A random mid-season race at Kansas.

explanation.summary: Crown jewels are the prestige races. Winning one, especially the Daytona 500, is a career highlight fans remember.

payload.prompt: Match each track to its personality.
payload.template: {{short}} is known for bumper-to-bumper short-track racing, while {{pack}} is known for pack racing.

explanation.correct: Right. Bristol is small and steep, so cars stack up nose to tail. Talladega is huge, so the draft makes packs.
explanation.incorrect: Bristol is the tight, bumper-to-bumper short track. Talladega is a giant superspeedway where drafting creates packs. Sonoma and Watkins Glen are road courses, and Martinsville is another short track.

payload.prompt: Does being great at one track type guarantee success at all?

scene.alt: Grid showing four different track types: short, intermediate, superspeedway and road course.

choices.label: Yes, a great driver wins anywhere

explanation.correct: Right. Even the best adapt, but a superspeedway ace is not automatically a short-track star.
explanation.incorrect: Track type matters a lot. A driver can be solid everywhere, but a road-course ringer may struggle at Bristol, and a short-track specialist may find Daytona a different game.
